title: Why a 5% Raise Can Still Leave You Poorer
alt_title_1: Irving Fisher & Amos Tversky on Escaping Money Illusion
alt_title_2: Nominal vs Real Wealth: Stop Celebrating Fake Dollar Gains
description_hook: Economist Irving Fisher coined 'The Money Illusion' in 1928, and Eldar Shafir, Peter Diamond, and Amos Tversky proved in a 1997 Quarterly Journal of Economics paper that our brains fixate on nominal dollar figures while ignoring real purchasing power. Here is the fix.

affiliate_cta.offer_name: Real Purchasing-Power Tracker + Economics Reading List
affiliate_cta.pinned_comment: Do you calculate your net worth and savings yield after inflation, or in raw nominal dollars? Grab our Real Purchasing-Power Tracker here: https://kenvh0010-lang.github.io/admin/bio/

scenes.headline: When a 5% Pay Bump Is Actually a 1% Pay Cut
scenes.stat_label: NOMINAL RAISE MINUS 6% INFLATION = REAL LOSS
bullets: Paystub shows more dollars hitting checking
Grocery and rent bills quietly outpace the raise
scenes.narration: Why does a five-percent salary raise during six-percent inflation feel like a victory, even though your real purchasing power just shrank?
scenes.source: Irving Fisher, The Money Illusion (1928); Shafir, Diamond & Tversky, QJE (1997)

scenes.headline: Irving Fisher (1928) & Tversky's 1997 QJE Proof
bullets: Fisher (1928): people mistake dollar units for static value
Shafir, Diamond & Tversky (1997): +5% in 4% inflation beat +2% in 0%
scenes.narration: Economist Irving Fisher named this Money Illusion in 1928. In 1997, Eldar Shafir, Peter Diamond, and Amos Tversky proved in the Quarterly Journal of Economics that people celebrate bigger nominal raises despite smaller real gains.
scenes.source: Shafir, Diamond & Tversky, 'Money Illusion', Quarterly Journal of Economics (1997)

scenes.headline: Idle Cash Looks Safe While Losing Real Ground
scenes.left_body: $20,000 in 0.1% checking -> steady digits, shrinking buying power
scenes.right_body: Measures yield & raises strictly net of inflation
scenes.narration: Watching raw dollar numbers tricks savers into leaving large balances in near-zero checking accounts, smiling at a steady number while inflation quietly erodes buying power.

scenes.headline: Subtract Inflation Before Celebrating Any Gain
scenes.stat_label: REAL RETURN = NOMINAL RETURN MINUS INFLATION
scenes.stat_subtext: Productive assets + high-yield reserves protect real margin
scenes.narration: Think strictly in real terms: subtract inflation from every salary bump, savings yield, and investment return before deciding whether your household actually moved ahead.

scenes.headline: Score Real Purchasing Power, Not Screen Digits
bullets: Move idle cash buffers into competitive real-yield accounts
Benchmark career and asset growth against real living costs
scenes.narration: Track real purchasing power after inflation, never flattering nominal numbers on a bank screen.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin principle based on Fisher (1928) and Shafir, Diamond & Tversky (1997)
